summary: Defines a YANG data model for configuring and managing Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD), conforming to the Network Management Datastore Architecture (RFC 8342). It updates the earlier BFD YANG model from RFC 9127. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: BFD is a quick heartbeat check between routers. This is a standard form for settings and watching that heartbeat from management software.

subtitle: A set of YANG modules for configuring BFD liveness sessions and reading their state, with an update to RFC 9127.

tldr.problem: Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD) runs over several kinds of paths, and each identifies its sessions differently. Operators need a standard way to configure BFD and read its state from management software.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a common BFD types module, a top-level module, and one module each for IP single-hop, IP multihop, LAG and MPLS LSP paths. All follow the NMDA, with configuration and state in the same tree.
tldr.outcome: It updates the model from RFC 9127. The main change is a new feature, client-base-cfg-parms, so BFD clients such as routing protocols can choose whether to carry per-session parameters.

facts.label: Path types covered
facts.value: IP single-hop, IP multihop, LAG, MPLS LSP

today: RFC 9314 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2022 and has not been obsoleted. It updates RFC 9127, and the unit metadata shows no later RFC updating it.

sections.title: What the Data Model Covers
sections.content:
This RFC defines YANG modules to configure and manage Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD, RFC 5880), a protocol used for liveness detection of arbitrary paths between systems. It covers BFD over single-hop IP (RFC 5881), multihop paths (RFC 5883), MPLS Label Switched Paths (RFC 5884) and Link Aggregation Group interfaces (RFC 7130). Pseudowires (RFC 5885) are explicitly not addressed.

BFD usually does not run alone. Control protocols called BFD clients use it, as described in RFC 5882. Likely clients are those without fast hellos, such as static routes, or whose hellos cannot detect failure in under a second, such as OSPF and IS-IS.

The modules follow the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA, RFC 8342), so there are no separate containers for configuration and operational state. The tree diagrams use the notation of RFC 8340.
sections.plainLanguage: Some network gear needs to notice quickly when a neighbor goes quiet. This document gives a standard way to tell it how, and to ask how it is doing.

sections.title: Module Layout
sections.content:
There is no single key that identifies a BFD session across all path types, so the model is split into modules, one per forwarding path. They differ mainly in how a session is uniquely identified. Common types and groupings avoid duplication.

A new control plane protocol, bfdv1, is defined, and a bfd container is created under control-plane-protocol from RFC 8349. Four modules augment that container:

  • ietf-bfd-ip-sh adds ip-sh for IP single-hop sessions.
  • ietf-bfd-ip-mh adds ip-mh for IP multihop sessions.
  • ietf-bfd-lag adds lag for sessions over a LAG.
  • ietf-bfd-mpls adds mpls for BFD over MPLS LSPs.

BFD can be used at the network-device level, where the model is used as is, or inside a logical network element or network instance, where it augments the mounted routing model.
sections.plainLanguage: There are different kinds of roads to watch. Each gets its own form, but all forms share the same common questions.

sections.title: Configuration and Session Identity
sections.content:
The configuration follows RFC 5880: local-multiplier, desired-min-tx-interval and required-min-rx-interval. Implementations may allow one interval for both directions, so the model offers a choice between a single min-interval and the separate pair. Authentication uses a key-chain reference (RFC 8177) and a meticulous flag.

What differs per path is the session key:

  • Single-hop: the interface and destination address pair.
  • Multihop: a session-group keyed by source and destination address, with tx-ttl and rx-ttl for outgoing and minimum incoming TTL. There may be several sessions per group because of multiple paths.
  • MPLS: a session group keyed by an IP prefix, for LSPs whose FEC is an IP address. The LSPs are unidirectional, so the egress node has no LSP configuration, and its BFD parameters sit under mpls.
  • LAG: one entry per LAG, with micro-BFD sessions on each member link and a destination address per address family.

BFD clients that auto-discover peers, such as IGPs, can use the client-cfg-parms grouping to create and remove BFD sessions with their own multiplier and intervals. How they do so is outside the scope of this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Each kind of road is named differently: by the two ends, by a group of lanes, or by a bundle of cables. The form also asks how often to check and how long to wait before worrying.

sections.title: Operational State, Notifications and Echo
sections.content:
The operational state holds overall statistics, such as the number of sessions and how many are up, down or admin-down, globally under bfd and per path type. For each session there are three categories of data: basics (local and remote discriminators, Demand mode capability), session-running data (remote state, diagnostic codes, negotiated intervals, detection time) and session-statistics (when it went up or down, and packet counts).

Notifications tell users about important events, such as a new session state, the time in the previous state and the reason for the change. They are defined per path type but reuse common groupings. The model defines no RPC operations.

RFC 5880 and RFC 5881 do not say whether the Echo function runs continuously or on demand, so starting and stopping it is implementation specific and should be done by augmentation, either by configuration or by an RPC. Appendix A gives an example module that adds an echo container with desired-min-echo-tx-interval and required-min-echo-rx-interval.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask each check-in line how many times it has gone down, and it can raise an alarm when something changes.

sections.title: Interaction With Other Modules
sections.content:
The BFD model depends on switches in other YANG modules. If /if:interfaces/if:interface/if:enabled from RFC 8343 is false, no BFD packets can be sent or received on that interface. In the same way, the IPv4 and IPv6 enabled and forwarding settings from the ietf-ip module block BFD packets of that address family, and the mpls-enabled setting from the ietf-mpls module blocks BFD MPLS packets.

The types module defines optional features that a server can declare: single-minimum-interval, authentication, demand-mode, echo-mode and the new client-base-cfg-parms. It also defines path-type identities for IP single-hop, IP multihop, MPLS and LAG, and the hops type, which corresponds to IPv4 Time To Live or IPv6 hop limit.
sections.plainLanguage: If the main switch for a cable is off, the tapping can not happen either. The form also lists extras that a device may or may not offer.

sections.title: Configuration Examples
sections.content:
Section 3 of the RFC gives NETCONF XML examples, one for each path type. Each sets the desired transmit and required receive interval to the same value:

  • IP single-hop on eth0: 10 ms.
  • IP multihop session group with an rx-ttl of 240: 150 ms.
  • LAG on Bundle-Ether1: 10 ms.
  • MPLS LSP: 250 ms.

In the XML the values appear in microseconds, for instance 10000 for 10 ms. The types module gives the multiplier a default of 3 and the intervals a default of 1000000 microseconds.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples are filled-in forms, showing a quick check every few thousandths of a second.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The modules are meant to be accessed with NETCONF (RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040), over SSH or TLS respectively, with access limited by NACM (RFC 8341).

Writable nodes can hurt the network if unprotected. The multiplier and interval nodes affect the session, address nodes can be used to send BFD packets to unwitting recipients, and the key-chain and meticulous authentication nodes affect session security. The system should police the creation of sessions so new ones do not cause existing sessions to fail.

For reads, the summary counters disclose session counts, including sessions the user cannot read. Access to the local and remote discriminators, combined with the authentication data, gives the ability to spoof BFD packets of that path type.
sections.plainLanguage: Only trusted people should be allowed to change or peek at the settings, since a stranger could use them to trick the check-ins.

sections.title: Updates Since RFC 9127
sections.content:
This document updates the ietf-bfd-types module with a new feature, client-base-cfg-parms, and an if-feature statement that conditionally includes parameters such as the multiplier and the desired minimum transmit interval. The module revision is marked as not backwards compatible with the previous one.

The feature lets implementations of protocols such as OSPF, IS-IS, PIM and BGP support both a model where those parameters are not needed, such as when multiple BFD sessions run over one interface, and one where they are defined per session. As a result, the BFD MPLS module uses base-cfg-parms instead of client-cfg-parms so it keeps all parameters unconditionally.

The iana-bfd-types module created in RFC 9127 is maintained by IANA, and no IANA changes are requested by this update.
sections.plainLanguage: The old form made every user fill in boxes that some did not need. The new form lets those boxes be switched off.
